# Introduction

During natural disasters such as typhoons and severe floods, real-time social media streams carry millions of messages about rescue needs, infrastructure damage, and relief offers [@imran2016twitter]. This volume outpaces manual review, so extracting critical information depends on automated natural language processing (NLP). This study formulates disaster triage as three concurrent NLP tasks. These comprise token-level named entity recognition (NER) for locations and infrastructure, sequence-level intent classification for humanitarian needs [@alam2021humaid], and sequence-level urgency prioritization of crisis messages [@wang2021transformerbased].

Serving one model per task multiplies latency and memory on local hardware. The study therefore adopts hard-parameter-sharing multi-task learning (MTL), which computes every prediction in a single forward pass. Joint training, however, couples heterogeneous task losses, and competing task gradients can degrade each task [@chen2018gradnorm; @yu2020gradient]. On low-resource, code-switched text, such joint training helped only under specific task pairings, training orders, and data sizes [@adouane2020when].

To resolve these computational and optimization challenges, this study develops an empirical benchmarking framework grounded in the Design Science Research Methodology (DSRM). The framework benchmarks seven candidate multi-task optimization (MTO) algorithms against uniform equal weighting (EW), tuned static linear scalarization (LS), and isolated single-task learning (STL) baselines. Evaluation covers Tagalog-English (Taglish) disaster tweets from four historical Philippine typhoons under a 4-fold leave-one-event-out (LOEO) protocol. The fine-tuned model is then deployed in a prototype web application for disaster triage.

## 1.1 Background of the Study

Disaster triage extracts three types of information from incoming crisis messages, namely location entities, humanitarian intent categories [@alam2021humaid], and urgency status [@wang2021transformerbased]. Deploying independent Transformer models for each task multiplies inference latency and parameter storage linearly as $\mathcal{O}(K)$ for $K$ tasks. In contrast, hard parameter sharing passes text through a shared multilingual Transformer encoder to compute intermediate contextual representations, which feed lightweight task-specific linear heads [@chen2024multitask; @ruder2017overview].

This unified architecture maintains near-constant inference latency ($\mathcal{O}(1)$ relative to $K$) on local workstation hardware. The shared encoder also introduces an inductive bias, because auxiliary tasks steer the model toward representations that explain more than one objective [@ruder2017overview].

Despite these architectural advantages, joint multi-task training introduces complex multi-objective optimization dynamics across shared parameters [@sener2018multitask]. When task loss gradients point in opposing directions ($\langle \mathbf{g}_i, \mathbf{g}_j \rangle < 0$), updating shared parameters along task $i$ increases the empirical loss on task $j$ to a first-order approximation. This condition produces destructive interference and negative transfer across shared layers [@liu2021conflictaverse; @navon2022multitask; @yu2020gradient]. Furthermore, when gradient scales diverge, tasks with larger gradient magnitudes dominate parameter updates and suppress secondary objectives [@chen2018gradnorm]. Joint models of token-level entities and sequence-level intent have improved performance on both tasks [@weld2022survey]. Achieving positive transfer ($\Delta_m > 0$) between NER and intent classification still requires principled gradient balancing. Whether such gains survive competing task gradients in a shared encoder remains an open empirical question.

Two primary MTO approaches address these optimization bottlenecks, namely dynamic loss weighting and gradient surgery. Dynamic loss-weighting algorithms adjust scalar task loss weights during training using distinct heuristics. Uncertainty weighting scales losses by learned homoscedastic uncertainty [@kendall2018multitask]. GradNorm balances gradient magnitudes against relative training paces [@chen2018gradnorm]. Fast Adaptive Multitask Optimization (FAMO) equalizes task loss decrease rates [@liu2023famo]. In contrast, gradient-surgery algorithms manipulate gradient vectors directly. Projecting Conflicting Gradients (PCGrad) projects conflicting gradients onto orthogonal normal planes [@yu2020gradient]. Conflict-Averse Gradient Descent (CAGrad) optimizes the worst-case objective improvement within a trust region [@liu2021conflictaverse]. Impartial Multi-Task Learning (IMTL-G) enforces equal-angle descent across objectives [@liu2021impartial]. Nash-MTL formulates gradient aggregation as a multi-objective bargaining game [@navon2022multitask].

Despite these theoretical motivations, empirical studies have shown conflicting evidence regarding whether dynamic MTO methods consistently outperform tuned LS or EW baselines. On machine translation and computer vision benchmarks, dynamic task weights often remained nearly constant during training, whereas per-task gradient computations reduced training throughput [@xin2022current]. Furthermore, under adaptive optimizers such as Adam, gradient magnitude disparities dominated multi-task updates, rendering vector surgery less effective and making EW competitive [@elich2024examining]. Because modern Transformer fine-tuning relies on AdamW, this study investigates whether these findings hold on low-resource code-switched text with asymmetric token-level and sequence-level objectives. To separate genuine cross-task conflict from stochastic mini-batch noise, the experimental framework computes pairwise gradient angles against an intra-task half-batch baseline [@elich2024examining].

In the Philippines, disaster response represents a critical operational priority. The Philippine Area of Responsibility experiences an average of 20 tropical cyclones each year, about eight or nine of which cross the country [@pagasaCyclone]. During major typhoon events, citizens broadcast large volumes of distress messages across social media. Prominent events include Typhoon Haiyan (2013), Typhoon Vamco (2020), Typhoon Rai (2021), and Typhoon Paeng (2022). Filipino disaster response has likewise adopted unified hashtags such as #RescuePH and #ReliefPH [@ermino2022evaluating]. Government agencies such as the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council and the Office of Civil Defense monitor these streams. However, locating urgent calls by manually scanning typhoon-related posts is less efficient than automated triage [@ermino2022evaluating].

Taglish introduces severe linguistic complexity into automated triage. Taglish crisis messages combine Tagalog and English in single sentences, along with misspellings, abbreviations, and slang [@herrera2022tweettaglish; @montalan2025batayan]. Formations such as "ma-evacuate" and "nag-collapse" illustrate Tagalog affixes applied to English roots. Multilingual Transformer tokenizers segment these morphologically hybrid words into fragmented subword sequences. For Tagalog, the examined tokenizers required between 1.74 and 3.28 subword pieces per word [@petrov2023language]. This fragmentation inflates sequence length and can dilute semantic embeddings and elevate gradient variance across shared layers. On other low-resource, code-switched text, joint training of sequence-labeling and classification tasks helped only in specific task configurations and did not benefit every task [@adouane2020when].

Operational constraints in Philippine disaster management further dictate deployment requirements. Local government units and municipal command centers frequently operate on commodity workstations subject to power grid failures and telecommunication outages during typhoons. Relying on cloud-hosted large language model APIs introduces critical risks. These risks include transmission latency, service loss during internet blackouts, recurring API costs, and compliance obligations under the Philippine Data Privacy Act of 2012 [@republic2012privacy]. Deploying compact, fine-tuned multi-task models locally provides a resilient, self-contained triage capability.

**Table 1.1**

*Structural Profile of Related Disaster Informatics and Philippine NLP Corpora*

|Dataset or Benchmark|Domain and Coverage|Modality and Corpus Volume|Language and Register|Annotation Level and Target Tasks|Cross-Event Evaluation Protocol|
|:-------------------|:------------------|:-------------------------|:--------------------|:----------------------------------|:-------------------------------|
|HumAID [@alam2021humaid]|Global crisis informatics (19 disaster events)|Text only (77,196 tweets)|Monolingual English (social media)|Sequence-level (11 humanitarian intent categories)|Event-stratified and cross-event splits|

*Note.* NLP = natural language processing. BIO = beginning, inside, outside. LOEO = leave-one-event-out.

As summarized in Table 1.1, existing benchmarks exhibit clear architectural limitations. Global crisis corpora such as HumAID provide large-scale intent annotations but remain restricted to monolingual English and lack token-level entity spans. Philippine NLP benchmarks, such as Batayan, TweetTaglish, and TLUNIFIED-NER, evaluate single tasks in isolation or focus on formal news text. No existing public corpus provides concurrent annotations for token-level named entities, sequence-level intent, and sequence-level urgency on Taglish crisis messages under cross-event evaluation.

The absence of such a corpus directly impairs multi-task optimization research for crisis triage. In a shared Transformer encoder, token-level NER aggregates cross-entropy loss across all subword tokens in a sequence, whereas intent and urgency classification computes loss over a single pooled representation. Token-level cross-entropy therefore sums over many more positions than pooled classification. Token labeling gradients can therefore dominate backpropagation ($\|\mathbf{g}_{\text{NER}}\|_2 \gg \|\mathbf{g}_{\text{Intent}}\|_2, \|\mathbf{g}_{\text{Urgency}}\|_2$). GradNorm targets exactly such magnitude disparities across tasks [@chen2018gradnorm]. Under EW, this structural asymmetry may allow token-level updates to overwrite pooled sequence representations, inducing negative transfer.

To address these empirical and optimization challenges, this study curates the Multi-Task Corpus of Taglish Disaster Tweets across four Philippine typhoons under a 4-fold LOEO protocol. The study evaluates dynamic loss weighting and gradient surgery against baseline methods, providing empirical guidance and an operational triage artifact for crisis informatics.

## 1.2 Statement of the Problem

This study addresses the general problem of accurate disaster triage for Taglish crisis messages on local workstation hardware. A separate single-task model for each task scales latency and memory linearly with task count ($\mathcal{O}(K)$ for $K$ tasks). A shared multilingual Transformer encoder reduces this cost to a single forward pass ($\mathcal{O}(1)$ relative to $K$). Joint training, however, couples heterogeneous task losses, and their gradients may differ in magnitude or point in opposing directions [@chen2018gradnorm; @yu2020gradient]. Such disparities and conflicts can induce negative transfer, leaving a joint model weaker than its single-task counterpart. Empirical evidence on these remedies remains conflicting. On translation and vision benchmarks, dynamic task weights stayed nearly constant and per-task gradient computations slowed training [@xin2022current]. Under adaptive optimizers such as Adam, magnitude disparities dominated updates and kept EW competitive, and stochastic mini-batch noise could be mistaken for genuine cross-task conflict [@elich2024examining]. Finally, no public corpus pairs token-level and sequence-level triage annotations on Taglish crisis text under cross-event evaluation. The study therefore investigates whether principled multi-task optimization, grounded in a curated Taglish disaster corpus, yields a triage model that is accurate, statistically validated, and deployable on local hardware.

To align the investigation with the DSRM lifecycle, the study decomposes this general problem into four specific problems:

1. **Specific Problem 1 (Phase 1, Baseline Analysis).** What baseline predictive scores do isolated single-task learning models establish on intent macro F1, urgency macro F1, and span-level NER F1? What baseline efficiency do these models establish in single-instance latency ($t_{\text{exec}}$ at $B=1$), throughput ($B=32$), and memory footprints ($M_{\text{VRAM}}$, $M_{\text{RAM}}$)? How do these metrics compare with a shared multilingual encoder under EW across 4-fold LOEO splits in predictive accuracy, gradient norm ratios ($R_{\text{max/min}}$), and pairwise gradient cosines?
2. **Specific Problem 2 (Phase 2, Design and Artifact Creation).** How should the hard-parameter-sharing pipeline, the candidate MTO algorithms, and the gradient diagnostic routines be designed to limit interference on Taglish text? How can the resulting model be integrated into a prototype web application for disaster triage?
3. **Specific Problem 3 (Phase 3, Empirical Benchmarking).** How do the seven candidate MTO algorithms compare with the STL, EW, and LS baselines across 4-fold LOEO splits? The candidates comprise dynamic loss weighting (Uncertainty Weighting, GradNorm, and FAMO) and gradient surgery (PCGrad, CAGrad, IMTL-G, and Nash-MTL). Which algorithms deliver the highest F1 scores, relative transfer ($\Delta_m$), and computational efficiency ($t_{\text{exec}}$, throughput, $M_{\text{VRAM}}$, $M_{\text{RAM}}$), and the shortest training runtime?
4. **Specific Problem 4 (Phase 4, Comparative Validation).** Are the observed performance differences among the MTO algorithms statistically significant under two-tier nonparametric testing with paired bootstrap confidence intervals and Friedman--Nemenyi tests? How strongly does relative transfer ($\Delta_m$) correlate with gradient conflict metrics measured against the intra-task half-batch baseline [@elich2024examining]?

## 1.3 Objectives of the Study

The general objective of this study is to construct the Multi-Task Corpus of Taglish Disaster Tweets and to benchmark candidate MTO algorithms on that corpus under 4-fold LOEO splits. The study further deploys the fine-tuned model in a prototype web application for disaster triage.

Aligned with these specific problems, the study pursues the following specific objectives:

1. **Specific Objective 1 (Phase 1, Baseline Analysis).** To establish the baseline predictive scores of isolated single-task learning models on intent macro F1, urgency macro F1, and span-level NER F1. To establish the baseline efficiency of these models in single-instance latency ($t_{\text{exec}}$ at $B=1$), throughput ($B=32$), and memory footprints ($M_{\text{VRAM}}$, $M_{\text{RAM}}$). To compare these metrics with a shared multilingual encoder under EW across 4-fold LOEO splits in predictive accuracy, gradient norm ratios ($R_{\text{max/min}}$), and pairwise gradient cosines.
2. **Specific Objective 2 (Phase 2, Design and Artifact Creation).** To design the hard-parameter-sharing pipeline, the candidate MTO algorithms, and the gradient diagnostic routines to limit interference on Taglish text. To integrate the resulting model into a prototype web application for disaster triage.
3. **Specific Objective 3 (Phase 3, Empirical Benchmarking).** To benchmark the seven candidate MTO algorithms against the STL, EW, and LS baselines across 4-fold LOEO splits. The candidates comprise dynamic loss weighting (Uncertainty Weighting, GradNorm, and FAMO) and gradient surgery (PCGrad, CAGrad, IMTL-G, and Nash-MTL). To identify the algorithms delivering the highest F1 scores, relative transfer ($\Delta_m$), and computational efficiency ($t_{\text{exec}}$, throughput, $M_{\text{VRAM}}$, $M_{\text{RAM}}$), and the shortest training runtime.
4. **Specific Objective 4 (Phase 4, Comparative Validation).** To test the observed performance differences among the MTO algorithms for statistical significance under two-tier nonparametric testing with paired bootstrap confidence intervals and Friedman--Nemenyi tests. To analyze the Spearman rank correlation ($\rho$) between relative transfer ($\Delta_m$) and gradient conflict metrics measured against the intra-task half-batch baseline [@elich2024examining].

## 1.4 Theoretical Framework

This study rests on three theoretical foundations, namely DSRM, complexity analysis of shared representations, and multi-objective optimization with gradient dynamics.

Unlike the behavioral sciences, which observe and predict natural phenomena, design science produces knowledge through the design, implementation, and empirical evaluation of computational artifacts. DSRM treats research as the creation and evaluation of artifacts that solve identified organizational problems. @hevner2004design required that such research produce a viable artifact, address relevant problems, apply rigorous methods, and yield clear, verifiable contributions. @peffers2007design formalized this inquiry as an iterative lifecycle of six activities. These are problem identification and motivation; definition of the objectives for a solution; design and development; demonstration; evaluation; and communication. The study operationalizes this lifecycle as four sequential phases, namely Baseline Analysis (Phase 1), Design and Artifact Creation (Phase 2), Empirical Benchmarking (Phase 3), and Comparative Validation (Phase 4). Under this foundation, the intellectual contribution comprises the empirical optimization findings and the curated corpus. The prototype serves as the demonstration artifact.

The second foundation combines asymptotic complexity analysis with the representation-sharing and inductive-bias principles described by @ruder2017overview. For $K$ tasks, single-task deployment executes $K$ forward passes per input, for a total cost of $\mathcal{O}(K \cdot T_{\text{sh}})$, where $T_{\text{sh}}$ is the backbone forward-pass time. Memory follows the same pattern, holding $K$ separate encoders at $\mathcal{O}(K \cdot |\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{sh}}|)$ parameters, where $|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{sh}}|$ is the encoder parameter count. Hard parameter sharing computes the shared representation once, reducing forward-pass time to

$$\mathcal{O}\left(T_{\text{sh}} + \sum_{k=1}^{K} T_{\text{head},k}\right)$$

where $T_{\text{head},k}$ denotes the head forward-pass time for task $k$. The linear heads are far cheaper than the backbone, so this total is effectively constant in $K$ ($\mathcal{O}(1)$ relative to $K$). Parameter memory likewise falls to

$$\mathcal{O}\left(|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{sh}}| + \sum_{k=1}^{K} |\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{head},k}|\right)$$

where $|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{head},k}|$ denotes the parameter count of the head for task $k$. The heads are linear layers with negligible parameter volume, so memory is also effectively constant in $K$. Beyond cost, the shared encoder restricts the parameter search to representations that explain more than one task, the inductive bias that auxiliary tasks provide.

The third foundation casts joint training as multi-objective optimization over the shared parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{sh}}$ and the task heads $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{head},1}, \dots, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{head},K}$ [@sener2018multitask]:

$$\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{sh}}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{head},1}, \dots, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{head},K}} \left( \mathcal{L}_1(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{sh}}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{head},1}), \dots, \mathcal{L}_K(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{sh}}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{head},K}) \right)$$

This formulation seeks Pareto-optimal configurations where no task loss can decrease without increasing another. Let $\mathbf{g}_k \equiv \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{sh}}} \mathcal{L}_k$ denote the gradient of task $k$'s loss with respect to the shared parameters. With learning rate $\eta$ and local smoothness, a first-order expansion of task $j$'s loss under a step along task $i$ yields

$$\mathcal{L}_j(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{sh}} - \eta \mathbf{g}_i, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{head},j}) = \mathcal{L}_j(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{sh}}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{head},j}) - \eta \langle \mathbf{g}_i, \mathbf{g}_j \rangle + \mathcal{O}\left(\eta^2 \|\mathbf{g}_i\|_2^2\right)$$

The linear inner product provides a first-order approximation under bounded learning rates, and the curvature residual remains bounded by $\mathcal{O}(\eta^2 \|\mathbf{g}_i\|_2^2)$ [@yu2020gradient]. @yu2020gradient used this decomposition to analyze when updates help or harm other tasks. Two failure modes follow.

**Disparity in Gradient Magnitudes.** When tasks label tokens and classify sequences at once, gradient magnitudes can diverge, and the larger gradient dominates the update, leaving smaller-gradient tasks behind [@chen2018gradnorm].

**Gradient Directional Conflict.** When the inner product is negative ($\langle \mathbf{g}_i, \mathbf{g}_j \rangle < 0$), the first-order term becomes positive, so a step along task $i$ raises the loss of task $j$, producing destructive interference [@yu2020gradient].

Section 1.1 presents the two MTO families that address these failure modes. Specialized MTO algorithms resolve them by projecting conflicting gradients onto orthogonal hyperplanes or by computing impartial descent directions. Following the diagnostic principle of @elich2024examining, the framework compares pairwise gradient angles with an intra-task half-batch baseline to separate genuine conflict from mini-batch noise. Per-fold paired bootstrap confidence intervals form the first validation tier. For the second tier, the Friedman test with its Nemenyi post-hoc procedure covers multi-model comparisons [@demsar2006statistical]. Both tiers are nonparametric. To translate these principles into an operational workflow, the study adopts the Input-Process-Output (IPO) conceptual framework.

## 1.5 Conceptual Framework

The IPO model structures the experimental design, algorithmic implementation, and empirical evaluation across the four DSRM phases. Figure 1.1 illustrates the overall conceptual framework of the research, and Figure 1.2 details the architectural workflow of the deployed software artifact.

**Figure 1.1**

*Overall Conceptual Framework of the Study*

![](figures/ipo-diagram-1.pdf)

### Input Stage

The input stage incorporates four core resources (I1 to I4). The first is the Multi-Task Corpus of Taglish Disaster Tweets partitioned across four historical typhoon events. The second covers four candidate Transformer encoders, three multilingual and one Tagalog-specific (XLM-RoBERTa, multilingual BERT, SEA-LION ModernBERT, and RoBERTa-Tagalog). The third spans optimization configurations from dynamic loss weighting and gradient surgery, benchmarked against single-task and static baselines. The fourth is a local workstation testbed running under FP16 mixed precision with a maximum sequence length of 128 and a training batch size of 32.

### Process Stage

The process stage executes four structured workflows (P1 to P4). The first covers text normalization, subword tokenization, BIO span alignment, and LOEO data splitting. The second covers multi-task fine-tuning and PyTorch gradient diagnostic logging against an intra-task half-batch baseline. The third applies two-tier nonparametric statistical validation, combining per-fold paired bootstrap confidence intervals with omnibus Friedman--Nemenyi ranking. The fourth embeds the fine-tuned model into an asynchronous FastAPI service with spatial gazetteer resolution.

### Output Stage

The output stage delivers four concrete research artifacts (O1 to O4). The first is a trained hard-parameter-sharing multi-task model executing concurrent predictions in $\mathcal{O}(1)$ time. The second produces validated empirical benchmark tables reporting task F1 scores, relative transfer ($\Delta_m$), computational efficiency, and gradient conflict dynamics across 12 paired evaluation runs. The third provides inferential bootstrap confidence intervals and nonparametric hypothesis test results. The fourth is a prototype web application for disaster triage supporting 4-stage incident lifecycle management.

**Figure 1.2**

*Architectural Workflow of the Deployed Software Artifact*

![](figures/ipo-diagram-2.pdf)

As shown in Figure 1.2, the software artifact operationalizes the trained multi-task model as an asynchronous FastAPI web service connected to a relational incident database (PostgreSQL). Disaster event replay streams and manual ingestion feed Taglish messages to the service, which executes single-pass concurrent inference for entity spans, humanitarian intent, and urgency labels. Extracted location and infrastructure entities are resolved against a local Philippine gazetteer dictionary, with an unmapped-span fallback for out-of-vocabulary toponyms. Recognized incidents are persisted with timestamps and tracked in an interactive dashboard across four operational lifecycle states (New, Acknowledged, Responding, and Resolved). This design lets municipal command centers triage, acknowledge, and monitor distress reports entirely on local infrastructure without cloud dependency.

## 1.6 Scope and Delimitations

### Scope of the Study

This study constructs the Multi-Task Corpus of Taglish Disaster Tweets. It benchmarks candidate MTO algorithms within a shared Transformer encoder. It then deploys the optimized model into a prototype web application for disaster triage. The experimental dataset targets 6,000 to 10,000 code-switched Taglish crisis tweets. A verified baseline of at least 6,000 annotated instances establishes the minimum corpus size. The tweets are drawn from four historical Philippine typhoons, namely Haiyan, Vamco, Rai, and Paeng. Evaluation follows a 4-fold LOEO cross-validation protocol. Each configuration runs across three random initialization seeds (42, 123, and 456).

The architectural scope covers encoder-only Transformer backbones under hard parameter sharing, spanning multilingual and Tagalog-specific models. The candidates are XLM-RoBERTa Base, multilingual BERT Base, SEA-LION ModernBERT, and RoBERTa-Tagalog Base. Hard parameter sharing spans the intermediate representations. Linear heads for token classification and sequence classification branch from the shared encoder. The optimization benchmark covers two algorithmic families. The first family is dynamic loss weighting, comprising Uncertainty Weighting, GradNorm, and FAMO. The second family is gradient surgery, comprising PCGrad, CAGrad, IMTL-G, and Nash-MTL. Both families are benchmarked against isolated STL, uniform EW, and static LS baselines.

Evaluation criteria comprise task F1 scores for intent macro F1, urgency macro F1, and CoNLL span F1 for NER. The criteria also include relative multi-task transfer ($\Delta_m$), unbatched latency ($t_{\text{exec}}$ at $B=1$), and batched throughput ($B=32$). Memory criteria cover peak GPU memory ($M_{\text{VRAM}}$) and host RAM ($M_{\text{RAM}}$), alongside training runtime. PyTorch gradient diagnostic hooks and an intra-task half-batch baseline track gradient norm disparities ($R_{\text{max/min}}$) and pairwise cosine similarities ($\cos(\mathbf{g}_i, \mathbf{g}_j)$). These diagnostics run on a local commodity GPU testbed. Statistical testing combines per-fold paired bootstrap 95% confidence intervals with omnibus Friedman--Nemenyi tests and Spearman rank correlation ($\rho$). The software deliverable provides an asynchronous FastAPI service, a relational incident database, and an interactive dashboard for crisis triage across four operational lifecycle states.

### Delimitations of the Study

To maintain methodological rigor and computational feasibility, the study sets clear operational boundaries. Linguistic analysis is confined to code-switched Taglish disaster text. The investigation excludes other Philippine regional languages, such as Cebuano, Ilocano, and Hiligaynon. Taglish constitutes the predominant register in Philippine disaster social media communications [@herrera2022tweettaglish]. Curating multi-task expert annotations across several regional languages would exceed the operational resource budget of this research. The corpus incorporates only public crisis microblogs collected from Twitter/X across four historical Philippine typhoons. These events are Typhoons Haiyan, Vamco, Rai, and Paeng. The study excludes private messaging platforms, non-crisis social media threads, and live platform streaming APIs. These exclusions prevent external API rate-limiting constraints and ensure deterministic experimental reproducibility through replayed historical datasets.

The data processing and inference pipelines handle raw textual content exclusively. They exclude multi-modal data streams such as satellite imagery, crowd-sourced photographs, voice recordings, and video feeds. In addition, the architectural scope is delimited to encoder-only Transformer backbones, both multilingual and Tagalog-specific. Those backbones use hard parameter sharing across intermediate representations. The investigation excludes soft parameter sharing, task-specific adapter modules, and proprietary cloud-hosted generative large language models. Such models require external network access and high-end server clusters.

Model evaluation covers the three primary triage tasks only. These tasks are token-level named entity recognition, sequence-level humanitarian intent classification, and sequence-level urgency prioritization. The study excludes auxiliary natural language processing tasks such as sentiment analysis, automatic summarization, and machine translation. The software deliverable serves strictly as an empirical research artifact and demonstration tool for local triage benchmarking. The application is not integrated into municipal emergency dispatch networks, live 911 infrastructure, or operational government command centers.

## 1.7 Significance of the Study

The outputs of this research deliver computational, methodological, and practical contributions to three distinct stakeholder groups.

**Disaster Response Agencies and Emergency Practitioners (Primary Beneficiaries).**  
Local emergency responders and municipal disaster offices gain a locally deployable triage system powered by a single shared Transformer encoder. The encoder executes named entity recognition, intent classification, and urgency prioritization in a single forward pass. The model therefore runs low-latency local inference on commodity workstations during electrical and telecommunication disruptions. Local deployment eliminates recurring cloud API fees. It also protects sensitive citizen communications in compliance with the Data Privacy Act of 2012 [@republic2012privacy]. Furthermore, the web prototype demonstrates automated entity extraction, local gazetteer mapping, and structured incident tracking. That tracking spans four operational lifecycle states.

**Machine Learning and Crisis Informatics Researchers (Secondary Beneficiaries).**  
Natural language processing researchers acquire the Multi-Task Corpus of Taglish Disaster Tweets. No surveyed corpus pairs concurrent token-level and sequence-level annotations on Philippine crisis text under cross-event evaluation, so the corpus fills that gap. In addition, researchers gain empirical benchmark evidence on dynamic loss weighting, gradient surgery, and static weighting. That evidence covers AdamW optimization on asymmetric natural language processing tasks. The PyTorch gradient diagnostic routines and the intra-task half-batch baseline provide a standardized methodology. That methodology separates genuine cross-task gradient conflict from mini-batch sample noise.

**Academic Institutions and Future System Developers (Tertiary Beneficiaries).**  
Academic institutions and system developers receive an open-source design science research artifact. The artifact contains modular training scripts, cross-event evaluation pipelines, and baseline model checkpoints. Future researchers can extend this framework to additional Philippine regional languages. They can also investigate post-training 8-bit or 4-bit quantization for edge devices, or integrate multi-modal sensor streams into the triage pipeline.

## 1.8 Definition of Terms

To establish technical precision across this study, the following terms are operationally defined. Each definition reflects the theoretical, mathematical, and algorithmic role of the term in the experimental framework and the software system.

**AdamW Optimizer.** An adaptive stochastic gradient descent optimization algorithm with decoupled weight decay. It maintains running exponential moving averages of first moments (gradient means) and uncentered second moments (uncentered gradient variances) for each parameter. In this study, the AdamW optimizer fine-tunes the shared Transformer backbone and the task-specific classification heads. It provides per-parameter gradient scale adaptivity across heterogeneous task loss landscapes. Decoupled weight decay maintains model generalization.

**BIO Schema for Token Annotation.** A token-level sequence labeling notation that marks the beginning (B-prefix), inside continuation (I-prefix), and outside tokens. Outside tokens carry the `O` tag without a prefix and belong to no named entity span. In this study, the schema structures token classification across five distinct tags. These are `B-LOC`, `I-LOC`, `B-INFRA`, `I-INFRA`, and `O`. The schema extracts multi-token location and infrastructure entities from code-switched Taglish disaster tweets.

**Computational Inference Latency ($t_{\text{exec}}$).** The median execution duration in milliseconds required for the multi-task model to execute a single forward pass. That pass outputs concurrent predictions for all three triage tasks under unbatched single-instance evaluation ($B=1$), computed as

$$\hat{t}_{\text{exec}} = \operatorname{median}\{\tau_1, \tau_2, \ldots, \tau_R\}$$

where $\tau_r$ is the elapsed time of timed repetition $r$, and $R$ is the count of timed repetitions recorded after warm-up. The benchmarking harness measures latency on CPU hardware, the deployment condition specified in Chapter 3. Results are reported as the median across timed repetitions.

**Design Science Research Methodology (DSRM).** An established research methodology in computer science and information systems. It creates and evaluates new artifacts to address practical operational problems. The artifacts here comprise a fine-tuned multi-task model, LOEO benchmark tables, and a FastAPI triage prototype evaluated against EW, LS, and STL baselines. In this study, DSRM organizes the research lifecycle into four sequential phases, namely Baseline Analysis, Design and Artifact Creation, Empirical Benchmarking, and Comparative Validation. The phases are structured under the IPO conceptual model.

**Disparity in Gradient Magnitudes ($R_{\text{max/min}}$).** The scalar ratio between the maximum and minimum $\ell_2$ norms of task gradients on shared encoder parameters at training step $t$, expressed as

$$R_{\text{max/min}}^{(t)} = \frac{\max_{k} \|\mathbf{g}_k^{(t)}\|_2}{\min_{k} \|\mathbf{g}_k^{(t)}\|_2}$$

In this study, this metric measures the degree to which dense token-level sequence labeling gradients dominate sparse sequence-level classification gradients during shared parameter updates.

**Dynamic Loss-Weighting Methods.** Multi-task optimization algorithms that dynamically adjust scalar task loss weights $w_k^{(t)} > 0$ at each training step $t$ to minimize the composite multi-task objective, formalized as

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}^{(t)} = \sum_{k=1}^K w_k^{(t)} \mathcal{L}_k^{(t)}$$

where $\mathcal{L}_k^{(t)}$ is the empirical loss for task $k$ at step $t$. The algorithms evaluated in this family are Uncertainty Weighting, GradNorm, and FAMO. They balance task learning rates during backpropagation by scaling scalar loss values. They do not modify gradient vector trajectories.

**FP16 Mixed Precision Execution.** A computational execution mode that performs forward and backward tensor operations using 16-bit half-precision floating-point arithmetic. The mode is managed through `torch.amp.autocast('cuda')` and `torch.amp.GradScaler('cuda')`. Master weights remain in 32-bit single-precision throughout. In this study, FP16 execution reduces peak GPU memory allocation ($M_{\text{VRAM}}$) and accelerates tensor throughput on the local workstation. It does so without compromising numerical gradient stability.

**Gradient Diagnostic Logging.** A diagnostic instrumentation procedure implemented through PyTorch gradient hooks. It computes and records per-task gradient norms ($\|\mathbf{g}_k\|_2$), gradient norm disparity ratios ($R_{\text{max/min}}$), and pairwise cosine similarities ($\cos(\mathbf{g}_i, \mathbf{g}_j)$) on shared encoder parameters. Recording occurs at every optimization step to track gradient conflict dynamics across training epochs.

**Gradient Directional Conflict.** A geometric condition in which gradient vectors for distinct tasks, taken with respect to shared parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{sh}}$, form an obtuse angle and produce a negative inner product, formulated as

$$\langle \mathbf{g}_i, \mathbf{g}_j \rangle < 0 \quad \text{or} \quad \cos(\mathbf{g}_i, \mathbf{g}_j) < 0$$

To a first-order approximation, the condition indicates that parameter updates along task $i$ increase the loss on task $j$.

**Gradient-Surgery and Projection Techniques.** Multi-task optimization algorithms that alter task gradient vectors $\mathbf{g}_k = \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{sh}}} \mathcal{L}_k$ before parameter updates. The alteration eliminates destructive cross-task interference. When pairwise gradient directional conflicts occur ($\langle \mathbf{g}_i, \mathbf{g}_j \rangle < 0$), these algorithms project conflicting vectors onto orthogonal hyperplanes or solve multi-objective subproblems. The family comprises PCGrad, CAGrad, IMTL-G, and Nash-MTL. Each member requires $K=3$ independent backward passes per optimization step.

**Hard-Parameter-Sharing Transformer Encoder.** A deep neural network architecture in which all three disaster triage tasks share the hidden representation layers of a single encoder-only Transformer backbone, either multilingual or Tagalog-specific. The backbone supports Taglish subword tokenization. The evaluated candidates are XLM-RoBERTa Base at approximately 279M parameters, multilingual BERT Base at approximately 178M parameters, SEA-LION ModernBERT at approximately 313M parameters, and RoBERTa-Tagalog Base at approximately 125M parameters. Dedicated task-specific classification heads branch from the shared encoder. The heads output entity spans, intent categories, and urgency labels in a single forward pass, yielding $\mathcal{O}(1)$ execution time relative to task count $K$.

**Inductive Bias in Representation Sharing.** The explicit optimization constraint imposed on a neural network by training shared encoder parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{sh}}$ across three concurrent loss functions. These functions are $\mathcal{L}_{\text{NER}}$, $\mathcal{L}_{\text{Intent}}$, and $\mathcal{L}_{\text{Urgency}}$. This shared objective restricts the parameter search space to representations that generalize across token-level and sequence-level triage tasks simultaneously. Generalization is measured as span-level NER F1 and macro F1 for intent and urgency under 4-fold LOEO evaluation on held-out typhoon events.

**Intra-Task Baseline Derived from Half-Batch Gradients ($\cos_{\text{intra}, k}$).** A diagnostic noise-floor metric computed as the cosine similarity between gradient vectors from two disjoint half-batches, $\mathcal{B}_k^{(1)}$ and $\mathcal{B}_k^{(2)}$, within the same task $k$, calculated as

$$\cos_{\text{intra}, k} = \frac{\langle \mathbf{g}_k^{(1)}, \mathbf{g}_k^{(2)} \rangle}{\|\mathbf{g}_k^{(1)}\|_2 \|\mathbf{g}_k^{(2)}\|_2}$$

In this study, this baseline provides an empirical reference threshold. The threshold distinguishes genuine cross-task gradient conflict from stochastic variance across mini-batch samples.

**Leave-One-Event-Out (LOEO) Cross-Validation.** A 4-fold cross-validation protocol in which models train on tweets from three historical disaster events and evaluate exclusively on the fourth held-out disaster event. Each configuration runs across three random initialization seeds, namely seeds 42, 123, and 456. Iterating across all four folds measures out-of-distribution generalization across distinct crisis environments.

**Macro-Averaged F1 Score for Sequence Classification.** The unweighted arithmetic mean of class-specific F1 scores across categorical sequence classification tasks. Those tasks are humanitarian intent with $|C_{\text{intent}}|=4$ and urgency priority with $|C_{\text{urgency}}|=2$, defined as

$$\text{Macro F1}_{\text{Task}} = \frac{1}{|C|} \sum_{c=1}^{|C|} \frac{2 \cdot P_c \cdot R_c}{P_c + R_c}$$

where $P_c$ and $R_c$ denote precision and recall for class $c$, computed from the pooled sequence representation $\mathbf{h}_{\text{pool}}$, such as $[\text{CLS}]$ or $\langle\text{s}\rangle$. The metric weights all target classes equally regardless of class frequency disparities.

**Multi-Task Corpus of Taglish Disaster Tweets.** The primary experimental dataset curated in this study. It targets 6,000 to 10,000 code-switched Taglish tweets, with a verified baseline of at least 6,000 instances. The tweets are collected across four historical Philippine typhoons under a 4-fold LOEO protocol. Each tweet contains three concurrent annotations. These are token-level BIO spans for location and infrastructure entities, sequence-level humanitarian intent classes, and sequence-level binary urgency labels. The binary urgency target derives from the four-level scale of @sarioglukayi2020detecting. That scale maps *Not Urgent* and *Somewhat Urgent* to the negative class and the two higher levels to the positive class. Annotations are validated through three independent judgments per tweet, and a label is approved when two of the three judgments agree.

**Multi-Task Inference Throughput.** The processing rate of the multi-task model during batched inference ($B=32$) on CPU hardware, expressed in tweets per second, computed as

$$\text{TP} = \frac{B}{\operatorname{median}\{\tau^{\text{batch}}_r\}}$$

where $B$ is the batch size and $\tau^{\text{batch}}_r$ is the elapsed time of batched repetition $r$. The benchmarking harness computes throughput from median batch times after warm-up, following the efficiency protocol of Chapter 3.

**Multi-Task Learning (MTL).** A machine learning approach in which a single neural network architecture with shared parameters is trained jointly across multiple related task objectives. The objectives here are token-level named entity recognition, sequence-level intent classification, and urgency classification. Joint training learns shared intermediate representations, improves generalization through inductive bias, and reduces inference latency relative to isolated single-task pipelines.

**Multi-Task Optimization (MTO) Algorithms.** Optimization algorithms, comprising dynamic loss-weighting methods and gradient-surgery techniques, that balance task gradients during backpropagation. These algorithms dynamically adjust task loss scalar weights $w_k^{(t)}$ or project shared gradient vectors $\mathbf{g}_k$ to optimize shared encoder parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{sh}}$.

**Negative Transfer.** An empirical condition in which joint multi-task optimization degrades generalization performance on task $k$ relative to an isolated single-task learning baseline, that is, $\text{F1}_{\text{MTL}, k} < \text{F1}_{\text{STL}, k}$. When destructive task interference predominates across all evaluated triage objectives, the composite relative transfer metric becomes negative ($\Delta_m < 0$).

**Nonparametric Hypothesis Testing.** Statistical inference procedures that evaluate performance differences between baseline and candidate models without assuming normally distributed metric distributions. In this study, the two-tier statistical framework establishes primary inferential validity through paired bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. Those intervals are computed across test instances within each held-out disaster fold. Omnibus repeated-measures Friedman tests with Iman-Davenport correction ($p < .05$) accompany them. Post-hoc Nemenyi critical difference ranking covers 12 paired event-seed runs, with an $N=4$ fold-level sensitivity analysis.

**Pareto Optimality in Multi-Task Learning.** A parameter state $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{sh}}^*$ in which no shared parameter update can decrease the empirical loss on task $i$ without increasing the loss on at least one other task $j$. Multi-task optimization algorithms seek parameter configurations along this Pareto frontier.

**Peak GPU Memory Allocation and Reservation ($M_{\text{VRAM}}$).** The maximum resident video memory in megabytes consumed by the neural network during training and batched inference on the GPU testbed. Tracking routines reset peak memory counters before each evaluation fold using `torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats`. They then record peak memory allocated and reserved during the fold. Allocation is read from `torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated`, and reservation is read from `torch.cuda.max_memory_reserved`.

**Peak Host Memory Usage ($M_{\text{RAM}}$).** The maximum resident set size (RSS) in megabytes of system RAM consumed by the host Python process during training and inference execution. It is measured programmatically as `psutil.Process().memory_info().rss / (1024 * 1024)` to quantify workstation deployment feasibility.

**Prototype Web Application for Disaster Triage.** The integrated software artifact developed as a functional research deliverable. It comprises an asynchronous FastAPI web service backend connected to a PostgreSQL relational database store. The backend executes single-pass inference and maintains timestamped crisis records. The artifact also comprises an interactive incident dashboard. The dashboard visualizes extracted entity locations through a local Philippine gazetteer dictionary with an unmapped-span fallback. It tracks incident lifecycle states across four operational stages, namely New, Acknowledged, Responding, and Resolved.

**Relative Multi-Task Transfer ($\Delta_m$).** A composite evaluation metric measuring the average percentage gain of multi-task model $m$ over isolated single-task baselines across all $K=3$ triage tasks, defined as

$$\Delta_m = \frac{1}{3} \sum_{k=1}^3 \left( \frac{\text{F1}_{\text{MTL}, k} - \text{F1}_{\text{STL}, k}}{\text{F1}_{\text{STL}, k}} \right) \times 100\%$$

where positive values ($\Delta_m > 0$) indicate positive transfer. Negative values ($\Delta_m < 0$) quantify net negative transfer.

**Sequence Labeling versus Sequence Classification.** The structural distinction between token-level dense prediction and sequence-level pooled prediction. Named entity recognition performs sequence labeling by aggregating cross-entropy loss over individual subword token hidden states $\mathbf{h}_t$. Intent and urgency classification perform sequence classification by predicting class distributions from the pooled sequence representation $\mathbf{h}_{\text{pool}}$. In multi-task training, this structural asymmetry causes gradient norm disparities between token-level and sequence-level tasks.

**Single-Task Learning (STL) Baseline.** A reference training configuration in which an independent Transformer model $\boldsymbol{\Theta}_k = \{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}, k}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{head}, k}\}$ is trained separately on each individual task $k \in \{\text{NER}, \text{Intent}, \text{Urgency}\}$, minimizing

$$\min_{\boldsymbol{\Theta}_k} \mathcal{L}_k(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_k)$$

These models establish empirical performance baselines ($\text{F1}_{\text{STL}, k}$). They also define the linear computational complexity baseline for inference latency, $\mathcal{O}(K \cdot T_{\text{sh}})$.

**Span-Level F1 Score for Named Entity Recognition (NER).** The harmonic mean of precision and recall computed over entity spans using the CoNLL evaluation standard, defined as

$$\text{Span F1}_{\text{NER}} = \frac{2 \cdot P_{\text{span}} \cdot R_{\text{span}}}{P_{\text{span}} + R_{\text{span}}}$$

A true positive requires an exact match on both the token span boundary $[t_{\text{start}}, t_{\text{end}}]$ and the entity category $E \in \{\text{Location}, \text{Infrastructure}\}$. Outside (`O`) tokens are excluded.

**Spearman Coefficient of Rank Correlation ($\rho$).** A nonparametric statistic that measures the monotonic association between two ranked variables, defined as

$$\rho = 1 - \frac{6 \sum_{i=1}^n d_i^2}{n(n^2 - 1)}$$

where $d_i = \text{rank}(x_i) - \text{rank}(y_i)$ denotes the rank difference for observation $i$, and $n$ represents the count of paired observations. In this study, $n=12$ across event-seed runs, or $n=4$ for fold-aggregated analysis. The coefficient evaluates monotonic relationships between gradient conflict metrics and relative multi-task transfer ($\Delta_m$).

**Static Linear Scalarization (LS).** A baseline multi-task optimization method that minimizes a fixed weighted sum of task losses, formulated as

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}} = \sum_{k=1}^K w_k \mathcal{L}_k$$

where the loss weights $\mathbf{w} = (w_1, \dots, w_K)$ remain constant during training. The weights are calibrated through a grid sweep across the simplex $\Delta^{K-1}$ under an equal hyperparameter search budget. The search uses an internal validation split carved from the training folds.

**Tagalog-English Code-Switching (Taglish).** The target linguistic register of Philippine disaster social media posts, characterized by intra-sentential and intra-word mixing of Tagalog morpho-syntactic elements and English lexical items. In this study, Taglish inputs combine Tagalog grammatical focus markers (*ang*, *ng*, *mga*, *sa*, and *na*). They also combine bound verbal affixes (*nag-*, *mag-*, *um-*, *i-*, and *-an*) with English root verbs and crisis terminology. This mixing induces subword fragmentation in standard multilingual tokenizers.

**Training Runtime.** The total wall-clock execution duration in seconds required to complete model fine-tuning across all training epochs on the GPU testbed. This metric accounts for optimization backward-pass requirements. Gradient-surgery algorithms require $K=3$ independent backward passes per step. Dynamic loss weighting and linear scalarization require a single joint backward pass.

**Uniform Equal Weighting (EW).** The default multi-task optimization baseline that assigns equal weight ($w_k = 1/K$) to all task losses, defined by

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}} = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^K \mathcal{L}_k, \quad \mathbf{g}_{\text{total}} = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^K \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{sh}}} \mathcal{L}_k$$

This baseline updates shared encoder parameters using the unweighted arithmetic mean of individual task gradients.
